CPI router and routing table \\nA router is a primary component of computer networks that connects \\nnetworks and is responsible for routing and forwarding datagrams. \\nDatagrams are usually forwarded through a network from one router to \\nanother until they reach their destination node. Similarly, CPI routers \\nare located at the nodes in a B2B e-commerce logistics network, such as \\nnodes representing transshipment centres, factories, and warehouses, as \\nshown in Fig. 1. They can not only deliver order and route information \\nthrough the cyber layer of the logistics network by routing and for-\\nwarding datagrams like traditional routers but also have logistics func-\\ntions for routing and forwarding the physical packages of logistics \\norders. \\nIn computer networks, routing and forwarding datagrams by routers \\nrequire updating route information and selecting the next hop through \\nrouting protocols, which rely heavily on routing tables, which are \\nessential data tables in routers. Routing tables contain topological in-\\nformation about neighbouring routers and networks and store infor-\\nmation about routes to specific network addresses and the routing \\nmetrics of the routes. While there are various routing protocols in a \\nrouting table, there are also different routing protocols within and \\namong ASs. Fig. 2(a) shows an example of a routing table for a computer \\nnetwork. \\nIn this work, we aim to route physical packages from sources to \\ndestinations through CPI networks; hence, the routing table in the CPI \\nrouter also plays a vital role in the routing process. Routers need to \\ndetermine the transportation routes of physical packages based on the \\ndatabase and routing protocols in the routing table. Therefore, based on \\nthe routing tables of computer networks, routing tables in CPI routers \\ninvolve logistic characteristics. Since the design of a complete routing \\ntable is outside the scope of this work, only the contents of the routing \\ntable related to this work are listed here, which mainly include desti-\\nnation, next hop, protocol, metric, and transportation information, as \\nshown in Fig. 2(b). In the routing table, destination refers to the IP \\naddress of the destination of a logistics order, and the next hop is the IP \\naddress of the next CPI router in the route to the destination. Protocol refers to the rules and basis for generating a transportation route for an \\norder. Transportation in the routing table refers to the transportation \\nmode along the route. \\nAmong the components of a routing table, routing protocols and \\nmetrics are the critical elements that are involved in routing decisions. \\nRouting protocols in computer networks facilitate the selection of the \\noptimal routes to ensure that datagrams can reach their destinations as \\nquickly as possible (Stavrou & Pitsillides, 2010). Metrics are essential for \\nevaluating the connectivity quality in the route selection process. \\nNevertheless, the use of metrics is directly related to the type of routing \\nprotocol applied in the networks. In most general terms, a metric is a set \\nof attributes of a route, consisting of any possible values used by the \\nrouting protocol to select the best route. When routing protocols are \\nused, they must guarantee route stability, and more importantly, the \\nselected routes should provide the optimal efficiency parameters (e.g., \\nhop counts, link quality parameters, and interference) within the ranges \\nof the selected attributes; thus, all these efficiency parameters can be \\nused as metrics in the routing table (Owczarek & Zwierzykowski, 2013). \\nSimilarly, in CPI networks, suitable metrics need to be selected to pro-\\nvide the optimal parameters of efficiency for the routing process in B2B \\ne-commerce logistics. On-time delivery of goods is essential for both \\nfactories and wholesalers, and choosing the shortest distance and fastest \\nmode of transportation could shorten the delivery time, satisfy buyers’ \\nneeds, and increase customer satisfaction. The transportation cost is an \\nimportant consideration in B2B e-commerce logistics. Choosing low-cost \\ntransportation options could reduce logistics costs and increase profit -\\nability. At the same time, wholesalers can also benefit from lower \\ntransportation costs, resulting in more competitive pricing. For B2B e- \\ncommerce, the time required for the transportation and delivery of \\ngoods is on the order of hours or days, whereas the time required for \\ninformation transmission in the routing process and the computation \\ntime for the routing decision are on the order of milliseconds or seconds \\n(Mao et al., 2017); hence, the information transmission time and \\ncomputation time are not the focus of this work (Sarraj et al., 2014a). \\nTherefore, important parameters in routing in B2B e-commerce logistics \\ninclude the distance and time for package transportation and the \\ntransportation cost, among others (Zhang et al., 2017), which are used \\nfor routing decisions as metrics in the routing table in this work. \\n4.CPI routing protocols \\nBased on the framework and components of the CPI networks pro-\\nposed in Section 3, this section focuses on modelling the routing prob-\\nlems and proposing routing protocols for B2B e-commerce logistics in \\nCPI networks.
